title: Distributional Shape of \(\hat{p}\) — When Does the CLT Kick In?

steps.instruction: In **Class Example 11.2** you used formulas to predict the *center* and *spread* of \(\hat{p}\). But a formula can't tell you the **shape** — that depends on the *success–failure condition*: \(np \ge 10\) **and** \(n(1-p) \ge 10\). This activity runs all three scenarios from 11.2 and lets you *see* the shape. The tool is already set to scenario **(a): \(p = 0.40\), \(n = 10\)**.
steps.observe: In 11.2, scenario (a) works out to \(np = 4\) and \(n(1-p) = 6\) — **both below 10**. Hold that thought for your prediction.

steps.instruction: Before drawing anything, reason from the success–failure condition for all three scenarios: **(a)** \(n=10, p=0.4\); **(b)** \(n=100, p=0.6\); **(c)** \(n=40, p=0.9\).

gate.question: Which scenario(s) will the CLT make look approximately **normal**?

choices.text: All three — the CLT always applies to proportions
**(a)** and **(b)** — because \(p\) is closest to 0.5 there

gate.feedback: Only **(b)** clears **both** \(np \ge 10\) and \(n(1-p) \ge 10\) (\(np=60,\ n(1-p)=40\)). Scenario (c) has a big \(np=36\) — but \(n(1-p)=4\) fails. Draw each one and watch.
gate.retryFeedback: Compute \(np\) **and** \(n(1-p)\) for each scenario. The rule needs *both* at least 10 — a large \(np\) alone isn't enough.

steps.instruction: Scenario **(a)** is already loaded (\(p=0.40,\ n=10\)). Tick **Show normal curve**, then click **+1000** three times (about 3000 studies).

requires.hint: Click **+1000** to draw at least 1000 samples of \(\hat{p}\), then continue.

steps.observe: Two things stand out: the bars are **chunky and granular** (only 11 possible \(\hat{p}\) values when \(n=10\)), and the pile is **right-skewed** — it doesn't hug the normal curve.
steps.reveal: With \(np = 4\) and \(n(1-p) = 6\), the success–failure condition **fails**, so \(\hat{p}\) is *not* normal. It's right-skewed (with \(p<0.5\), the longer tail points toward larger values) and granular because \(n\) is so small.

steps.instruction: Now set **Population proportion \(p\)** to **0.60**, then **Sample size \(n\)** to **100** (this clears the plot). Keep **Show normal curve** on and click **+1000** three times.

requires.hint: Set **\(n = 100\)** and **\(p = 0.60\)**, then click **+1000** to fill the new distribution.

steps.observe: This time the pile is a smooth, symmetric **bell** that tracks the normal curve closely.
steps.reveal: Here \(np = 60\) and \(n(1-p) = 40\) — **both well above 10** — so the CLT applies and \(\hat{p}\) is approximately normal. Your **{{samples}}** draws gave an SD of \(\hat{p}\)'s of **{{statSD}}**, matching the theory value \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n} = \) **{{theorySE}}**.

steps.instruction: Last one — the case to watch. Set **\(p\)** to **0.90**, then **\(n\)** to **40** (this clears the plot), and draw **+1000** three times.

requires.hint: Set **\(n = 40\)** and **\(p = 0.90\)**, then click **+1000** to fill the new distribution.

steps.observe: Even though \(n=40\) is *larger* than scenario (a)'s, the shape is clearly **left-skewed** — a long tail toward smaller values, bunched against the ceiling at 1.0.
steps.reveal: This is the trap. \(np = 36\) is large, so it's tempting to call it normal — but \(n(1-p) = 4\) **fails**, and that alone keeps it skewed. The condition is an *and*, not an *or*: a large \(np\) can't rescue a small \(n(1-p)\).

steps.instruction: You've now seen all three shapes. Put the pattern into your own words before the summary.

prompts.label: Why is (c) skewed even though \(np = 36\) is large?

respond.answer: Only **(b)** is normal. **(a)** is right-skewed and granular (\(np=4,\ n(1-p)=6\), tiny \(n\)); **(c)** is left-skewed because \(n(1-p)=4\) fails, even though \(np=36\) is large. The rule is an **and**, not an **or** — both \(np\) and \(n(1-p)\) must reach about 10.

steps.reveal: The sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is only approximately normal when **both** \(np \ge 10\) and \(n(1-p) \ge 10\). When either part fails, the shape skews toward whichever boundary (0 or 1) that \(p\) sits nearer — right-skew for small \(p\), left-skew for large \(p\) — and a small \(n\) also makes it granular. That's why (b) looks normal while (a) and (c) don't, confirming the conditions you checked in Example 11.2.
